extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and the informed public debating the proposed U.S. Constitution; legislators and jurists interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative exposition on the design, scope, and practical operation of the federal judiciary under the proposed U.S. Constitution, focusing on appellate jurisdiction, concurrent state jurisdiction, and the role of jury trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction 'both as to law and fact'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court is said to possess appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact; it may not institute a new inquiry into fact but takes cognizance of the fact as it appears upon the record and pronounces the law arising upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutes jurisdiction of both fact and law; expressions saying 'appellate jurisdiction, both as to law and fact' do not necessarily imply re‑examination of facts decided by juries in inferior courts. Such appellate power should be understood broadly but subject to legislative exceptions and regulations to avoid practical injustices (e.g., preserving jury trials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction subject to legislative exceptions and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court should be declared generally 'both as to law and fact' but made subject to such exceptions and regulations as the national legislature may prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing the clause generally allows the legislature to qualify it (for example, to bar re‑examination of facts tried by juries) so the government can modify appellate practice to best serve public justice and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State courts retained unless exclusively delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will retain their pre‑existing authorities unless those powers are exclusively delegated to the federal head by the Constitution (in express terms, by prohibition, or by incompatibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, State courts should have concurrent jurisdiction in many cases arising under federal law, and appeals from State courts to the Supreme Court should be available to prevent elusion of federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional discretion to constitute inferior courts and define their authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is authorized to constitute tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court and may determine whether subordinate courts have original or appellate jurisdiction (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Constitution outlines federal judicial power but not the precise role of inferior courts, Congress may create appellate routes (including appeals from State courts to subordinate federal tribunals) to manage caseloads and shape the appellate structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: An appeal may lie from State courts to subordinate federal tribunals (legislative option)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no constitutional impediment to establishing appeals from State courts to subordinate national tribunals; this could reduce the need for many federal courts and allow flexibility in appellate organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such arrangements could contract Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction and leave State tribunals more of the charge of federal causes while providing intermediate appellate review in district courts when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence in the Constitution does not abolish trial by jury in civil cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's failure to mention jury trials in civil cases does not imply their abolition; silence is not equivalent to prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit provision for trial by jury in criminal cases does not deprive the legislature of the power to authorize jury trials in civil cases; legal maxims used to argue otherwise are misapplied here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute courts includes prescribing the mode of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative power to create courts carries with it the discretion to prescribe the mode of trial (jury or otherwise) for causes within those courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nothing were said about juries, Congress could choose whether to employ them in civil cases; the express injunction for criminal juries limits that discretion only in criminal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'As heretofore' formulations are impractical for a federal provision
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional clause saying 'trial by jury shall be as heretofore' would be meaningless at the federal level because there is no single antecedent federal practice to which 'heretofore' could refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because jury practice varies materially among the States, attempting to fix one State's practice as the federal standard (or to refer vaguely to past practice) would be senseless or inoperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juries are unsuitable for certain specialized cases (e.g., prize causes, laws of nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases that turn wholly or largely on the laws and usages of nations (such as prize causes) are inappropriate for jury determination because juries lack the necessary specialized knowledge and may be swayed by impressions contrary to considerations of public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such matters may require re‑examination of fact and law in a manner inconsistent with ordinary jury trials and may be handled differently (as in European practice where facts and law are re‑examined in high tribunals) to avoid endangering public peace or foreign relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction generally incompatible with jury trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity address extraordinary, intricate cases and require long, deliberate, and critical investigation incompatible with the mode and aims of jury trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping equity and law jurisdictions separate preserves the integrity of both; committing equity causes to juries would unsettle general rules and risk undermining the trial by jury by introducing complex issues unsuitable for jurors called from ordinary occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury as a safeguard against corruption (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial by jury is a valuable check against corruption because it is harder to tamper with a dispersed temporary jury than with standing magistrates; when courts and juries both function, there is double security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection is real though diminished by possibilities of corrupting officials who select jurors (sheriffs, clerks). Nonetheless, the combination of jury and judicial oversight (e.g., new trials) increases obstacles to successful corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury trials may be impractical or harmful for revenue/tax collection procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary procedures (distress and sale) are commonly used for tax collection because jury trials would be dilatory and add costs that could exceed the tax owed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain effective revenue enforcement and practical governance, some summary non‑jury procedures are necessary; the existence of jury trial protections in criminal cases suffices to guard against official extortion related to revenue enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of interpretation: specification of particulars excludes generals, but must follow common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal maxims like 'specification of particulars excludes generals' have meaning, but their application must conform to common sense and the nature of the instrument being construed; they cannot be perversely applied to infer abolition where silence exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional provisions should be read in their natural and obvious sense rather than through strained technical maxims; examples show enumeration limits scope, but that principle must be used reasonably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate limitation of Supreme Court original jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan carefully restricts the judicial authority vested originally in the Supreme Court (only a small portion preserved as original), consigning most original jurisdiction to subordinate tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distribution, with a broad appellate role for the Supreme Court and legislative power to shape inferior courts, aims to balance national and local adjudication while avoiding concentration of original federal judicial power.
